opus-5.5.text:
I think the potential is actually very large, and in a way robotics is one of the areas where the two countries are naturally complementary.

If you look at the strengths on each side, the US has been very strong in the foundational research, especially in AI. A lot of the recent progress in robot learning, foundation models, large-scale simulation, and reinforcement learning came out of labs and companies in the US. On the other hand, China has an incredible advantage in hardware and manufacturing. The supply chain for motors, actuators, batteries, sensors, all the components that go into a robot, is extremely mature in China. You can iterate on a hardware design there in weeks, where elsewhere it might take months. And cost matters enormously for robotics, because if we want robots to really go into homes and factories at scale, they have to be affordable.

So when you put these together, the brain and the body, so to speak, I think that's how we get to general-purpose robots faster. Robotics is fundamentally a hard problem. It's not just software; you have to deal with the physical world, with friction, contact, uncertainty. No single country or single company is going to solve it alone.

I'd also say the research community itself is already very international. Many of the people working on robot learning in the US are originally from China, and there's a lot of exchange through papers, open-source code, and conferences. Open-source datasets and models have been especially important; when one group releases something, everyone around the world builds on it the next week. That kind of openness has really accelerated the field.

Of course, I'm not naive about it. There are real geopolitical tensions, export controls, and concerns about security, and those create friction. But from the perspective of a researcher, I hope that at least at the level of science and open knowledge, the collaboration can continue. The goal of building robots that can help people, help with aging populations, labor shortages, dangerous jobs, these are challenges that both societies face. I think robotics could benefit humanity much more if we work on it together rather than in isolation.

r001.rationale: The response says the US is strong in foundational research and AI, while China has an advantage in robotics hardware and manufacturing, describing the two as complementary.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about this question a lot, actually, because I've lived on both sides of it. I did my undergraduate work in China, and then I spent most of my career in the US, at Georgia Tech and then at Google, working on legged robots and learning-based control. So when people frame this as a competition, I understand why, but I think the framing misses what's actually happening in the field.

Robotics right now is at a really interesting moment. For a long time, the bottleneck was hardware. Motors, batteries, sensors, actuators. And China has become extraordinarily good at that part. If you look at Unitree, or the supply chain around Shenzhen, the cost of a capable quadruped or a humanoid platform has dropped by an order of magnitude in just a few years. That is not a small thing. In my own work, when we wanted to test a new learning algorithm on real legged robots, the cost and availability of the hardware directly determined how many experiments we could run. Cheaper, better hardware accelerates the whole research cycle.

On the other side, a lot of the foundational work in learning-based control, sim-to-real transfer, and now these large foundation models for robotics has come out of US labs and companies. The ideas about how you train a policy in simulation and get it to work on a physical robot, how you scale data collection, how you connect language and vision models to low-level control, much of that originated in the US ecosystem.

So you have two complementary strengths. Hardware and manufacturing capacity on one side, and a lot of the algorithmic and model-scale innovation on the other. In principle, that's a natural partnership. And honestly, in practice, it already is, more than people realize. Research papers are open. Code is open. Many of the researchers in top US robotics labs are Chinese or Chinese-American. When I go to conferences like CoRL or RSS, the conversations between Chinese and American researchers are completely normal. People share results, they build on each other's work, they argue about methods. Science at that level doesn't really have borders.

Where it gets complicated is at the level of policy and industry. Export controls, concerns about dual use, investment restrictions. I'm not naive about that. Robotics touches national security in ways that, say, recommendation systems don't. And I think both governments are going to continue to be cautious.

But I'd make two points. First, robotics is fundamentally about solving physical problems that every society has. Aging populations, labor shortages in manufacturing and logistics, dangerous work that humans shouldn't have to do. China and the US face those problems in very similar ways. The incentive to solve them is shared.

Second, the hardest problems in robotics are still unsolved. We don't have robots that can reliably do general-purpose manipulation in an unstructured home. We don't have the data infrastructure that language models had with the internet. These are problems that are big enough that no single country is going to solve them alone, and I think the researchers on both sides know that.

So my honest view is that collaboration will continue to happen at the academic and open-source level, probably more than headlines suggest, while being constrained at the commercial and governmental level. And I'd argue the field is better off the more we can protect that first channel. The progress we've seen in the last five years, in legged locomotion, in learned manipulation, came from an open, global research community. I'd hate to see that fragment.

r001.rationale: It describes Chinese strengths in hardware and manufacturing alongside U.S. strengths in robotics algorithms and model-scale innovation, and calls them complementary.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s tremendous potential. Robotics brings together so many disciplines—AI, hardware, manufacturing, and control—that progress depends on people with different strengths working together. China and the United States have a lot to contribute, and there are shared challenges where collaboration could be valuable: helping older adults live independently, making workplaces safer, and building robots that can reliably assist people in everyday life.

Of course, we have to recognize that there are concerns around security and trust. I wouldn’t assume collaboration will be easy in every area. But exchanging ideas through academic research, developing common safety standards, and working on clearly beneficial applications seem like constructive places to start. My hope is that researchers can keep those connections open and focus on problems where progress benefits people in both countries.

r001.rationale: The response says both countries have different strengths and mentions AI, hardware, and manufacturing generally, but it does not identify U.S. robotics intelligence development as a strength and Chinese robotics hardware manufacturing as a complementary strength.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s tremendous potential. Robotics brings together many different strengths, from research and software to hardware and manufacturing. Collaboration between China and the United States could help turn promising ideas into robots that are useful in everyday life.

A good starting point is shared technical challenges: making robots safer, more reliable, and better able to operate in unfamiliar environments. Researchers can exchange ideas, develop common benchmarks, and learn from one another’s experiments.

Of course, there are concerns around intellectual property, security, and trust. We should take those seriously and define clear boundaries. But I’m hopeful that we can preserve meaningful collaboration, especially on applications where the benefits are widely shared.

r001.rationale: The response mentions robotics research, software, hardware, and manufacturing as broad areas of strength, but does not attribute intelligence development to the U.S. and hardware manufacturing to China.
